title: Roots of complex numbers
subject: Pure Mathematics
summary: A complex number is a point with a distance (modulus) and a direction (argument). Roots are found by De Moivre’s theorem: take the root of the modulus, divide the angle, and spread the roots evenly round a circle.

notes.title: Modulus and argument
notes.text: A complex number z = x + yi is the point (x, y). Its modulus |z| = √(x² + y²) is its distance from the origin. Its argument is the angle from the positive real axis (anticlockwise is positive). Example: {k1} {s1*k1|s}i has modulus {k1}√2 and argument {45*s1}°.
notes.hint: Sketch the point. The distance uses Pythagoras, and the angle comes from the quadrant.

notes.title: Cube roots: the modulus
notes.text: If z = r(cos θ + i sin θ), every cube root has modulus ∛r and argument (θ + 360°k) ÷ 3 for k = 0, 1, 2. So there are always three different cube roots. Example: if |z| = {m1*m1*m1}, each cube root has modulus {m1}.
notes.hint: Which number multiplied by itself three times gives the modulus?

tasks.q: |z| = {m3}. What is the modulus of each cube root?
why: Cube-rooting is not multiplying by 3.
Cube-rooting is not adding 3.
{m3} is the modulus of z itself. Take its cube root.

notes.title: Cube roots: the angles
notes.text: Put k = 0, 1, 2 into θₖ = (θ + 360°k) ÷ 3, then bring each angle into (−180°, 180°]. Divide the whole bracket by 3. Example: θ = {ph1}° gives θ₀ = {ph1/3}°, θ₁ = {(ph1+360)/3}° and θ₂ = {ph1/3-120}°.
notes.hint: θ₀ = θ ÷ 3. For θ₁, add 360° first, then divide by 3.

tasks.q: A number has argument θ = {ph}°. Enter the arguments θ₀ (k = 0) and θ₁ (k = 1) of its cube roots.

fb.{ph},{ph+360}: Divide the whole angle by 3: θ₀ = {ph} ÷ 3 and θ₁ = ({ph} + 360) ÷ 3.

notes.title: Evenly spaced roots
notes.text: The n roots of a number all have the same modulus and are spaced evenly round a circle, 360° ÷ n apart. Example: for n = {n1} the roots are {360/n1}° apart.
notes.hint: A full turn is 360°. Share it equally between the roots.

tasks.q: How far apart (in degrees) are neighbouring roots when you take the {n}th root of a number?
why: 180° is half a turn, so that halves the gap.
720° is two full turns, so that doubles the gap.

exercises.q: How many distinct {n}th roots does a non-zero complex number have?
why: There are exactly {n}, evenly spaced.
